disclaimer: Disease information is compiled from public agricultural extension and research sources for educational purposes. It is not a substitute for professional plant-pathology diagnosis. Treatment recommendations should be verified against local agricultural advisories before use.

diseases.description: Apple scab is a fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis that affects apple trees worldwide. It causes lesions on leaves, fruit, and twigs and can reduce fruit quality and yield.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown lesions on leaves
Lesions may be circular or irregular
Severe infection can cause premature leaf drop
visual_signs: Dark olive or brown velvety spots on upper leaf surfaces
Raised scab lesions on fruit skin
Cracked, corky appearance of infected tissue
prevention: Remove and destroy fallen leaves and infected fruit
Apply appropriate fungicide programs during the growing season
management: Fungicide sprays timed to primary infection periods
sources: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic — Apple Scab
Penn State Extension — Apple Disease Management
treatment: Sanitation first: rake and destroy fallen leaves and remove mummy fruit — most inoculum overwinters on ground debris.
Prune for an open canopy so leaves dry quickly after rain.
Apply a protective fungicide program from green tip through the primary spring infection period; continue cover sprays while scab is active.
Plant resistant cultivars for future plantings.

pesticides.application: Start at green tip and maintain cover sprays (typically every 7-14 days per label, shortened after rain) through the primary infection period. Rotate modes of action between groups and observe the pre-harvest interval.

diseases.description: Black rot is a fungal disease that affects apple trees, causing leaf lesions, fruit rot, and cankers on branches and trunks.
symptoms: Brown leaf spots with concentric rings (frog-eye appearance)
Fruit rot starting at the calyx end
prevention: Prune out dead or cankered wood
management: Fungicide applications during bloom and post-harvest
treatment: Prune out cankers, dead wood, and branch stubs during dry weather — branch cankers are the main inoculum source.
Remove and destroy all mummified fruit and fallen leaves.
Avoid tree wounds; manage bird and rodent damage that creates entry points.
Apply fungicide during the growing season where the disease has been active, and protect fresh pruning wounds.

pesticides.application: Spray at pink and again at petal fall where black rot or scab pressure exists, with follow-up cover sprays per label during warm, wet weather; dormant applications for canker control where the label allows.

diseases.description: Cedar apple rust is a fungal disease that requires both apple and juniper (cedar) hosts. It causes bright orange-yellow spots on apple leaves and can defoliate trees.
symptoms: Bright orange-yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces
visual_signs: Vivid orange or yellow leaf spots
Coral-like galls on juniper branches (alternate host)
Orange, finger-like projections on apple leaf undersides
prevention: Remove nearby juniper/cedar alternate hosts when practical
Apply fungicides during the infection window
management: Fungicide programs timed to juniper telial stage
Avoid planting apples near junipers in new orchards
treatment: Remove the alternate host where practical: cut down juniper/cedar trees within a few hundred metres — the fungus cannot complete its life cycle without both hosts.
Remove galls from remaining junipers and prune out infected apple twigs.
Collect and destroy fallen infected leaves and fruit.
Apply protective fungicide on apple during the spring infection window (teliospore release follows rainy weather).

pesticides.application: Myclobutanil is the most effective option: start at pink and continue per label through roughly petal fall plus 2-3 weeks. Sulfur and copper are protectants with shorter residual activity. Observe the pre-harvest interval.

Powdery mildew is a fungal disease affecting cherry leaves and fruit, characterized by white powdery fungal growth.
symptoms: White powdery coating on leaves and shoots
visual_signs: White to gray powdery fungal growth on leaf surfaces
management: Fungicide applications during the growing season
treatment: Prune for an open canopy and avoid excessive nitrogen fertilisation — succulent growth is most susceptible.
Apply fungicide from shuck split through the summer where pressure is high (warm days with humid nights favour the disease).
Prune out and destroy heavily infected shoots where practical.

pesticides.application: Cover sprays from shuck split at label intervals; rotate the systemic groups (myclobutanil, triflumizole) with sulfur or potassium bicarbonate to slow resistance. Sulfur can burn foliage/fruit at high heat, and pre-harvest intervals matter on ripe fruit.

diseases.description: Cherry leaf tissue with no visible symptoms of the diseases supported by this model.

diseases.disease: Cercospora Leaf Spot / Gray Leaf Spot
diseases.description: Gray leaf spot is a significant fungal disease of maize caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis, producing elongated rectangular lesions on leaves.
symptoms: Elongated, rectangular lesions parallel to leaf veins
Lesions turn gray to tan as they mature
visual_signs: Rectangular gray-brown lesions bounded by leaf veins
Lesions may coalesce in severe cases
management: Fungicide applications when threshold conditions are met
treatment: Manage crop residue: bury or remove infected stalks and leaves — the fungus overwinters on residue.
Rotate with non-host crops (soybean, small grains) for 1-2 years.
Plant resistant or tolerant hybrids where available.
Scout the lower canopy from V6; apply fungicide when lesions reach the ear leaf before or at tasseling under warm, humid conditions.

pesticides.application: Time application at VT-R1 (tasseling to silking) when at least half of plants show lesions on the ear leaf or above, especially on hybrids with intermediate or low resistance. Rotate FRAC groups between applications — strobilurin resistance in Cercospora is documented in several regions.

diseases.description: Common rust of corn is caused by Puccinia sorghi and produces reddish-brown pustules on leaf surfaces.
symptoms: Pustules appear on both leaf surfaces
Severe infection can cause leaf yellowing and premature death
prevention: Early planting to avoid peak spore periods
management: Fungicide use in high-value or severe infection situations
treatment: Plant resistant hybrids — the most economical control; resistance genes are widely available.
Scout from early vegetative stages; rust usually appears first on lower leaves as cinnamon-brown pustules.
Fungicide is rarely needed for field corn grown for grain; consider it for seed corn or sweet corn when disease is actively progressing before grain fill under cool, moist weather.

pesticides.application: Apply at early leaf stages if scouting shows active pustule development and yield potential is high; keep label intervals and rotate strobilurins with triazoles. Applications after grain fill are generally not economic for field corn.

diseases.description: Northern leaf blight is a fungal disease of maize producing large cigar-shaped lesions on leaves.
visual_signs: Elliptical lesions up to several inches long
management: Fungicide applications when disease pressure warrants
treatment: Rotate with non-host crops and use tillage to bury infected residue — sporulation requires residue.
Plant hybrids carrying Ht resistance genes.
Scout for cigar-shaped lesions from V6; fungicide pays on continuous corn with susceptible hybrids when lesions appear before tasseling under cool, humid conditions with long leaf wetness.

pesticides.application: Apply at VT-R1 when the majority of plants have lesions reaching the ear leaf on susceptible hybrids; intervals are often 14-21 days per label. Rotate modes of action between applications.

Black rot is a major fungal disease of grapes causing fruit rot, leaf lesions, and cane infections.
symptoms: Circular leaf lesions with dark borders
Fruit shriveling into hard black mummies
visual_signs: Tan leaf spots with purple-brown borders
prevention: Remove mummified fruit and infected canes
management: Fungicide program from bloom through fruit development
sources: Penn State Extension — Grape Disease Management
treatment: Prune out and destroy mummified berries, infected tendrils and trunk cankers — mummies are the overwintering inoculum.
Remove wild grapes and keep an open canopy so clusters dry quickly.
Apply a strict protectant program from bud swell through bunch closure (the critical window); sprays after infection do not cure already-infected berries.
Bury or remove fallen leaves.

pesticides.application: Protectant program: start at bud swell and continue at label intervals (7-14 days, shorter after rain) through bloom and bunch closure. Myclobutanil gives limited eradicant action early but cannot cure established infections. Rotate groups and respect the PHI before harvest.

diseases.description: Esca is a complex grapevine trunk disease involving several fungal pathogens. It causes leaf stripes, tiger-stripe patterns, and vine decline.
symptoms: Tiger-stripe pattern on leaves (interveinal chlorosis and necrosis)
visual_signs: Yellow and brown interveinal striping on leaves
Red-brown wood with white sectors in cross-section
treatment: No reliable chemical cure exists for this trunk disease; management is by vine surgery and wound protection.
Prune out symptomatic wood during dormancy, cutting back to clean wood well below visible lesions; tiger-striped leaves signal affected cordons.
Protect all pruning wounds immediately with a registered wound protectant (for example Trichoderma-based formulations where they are registered).
Remove and replace vines with severe trunk lesions; avoid mechanical injury, drought stress and excessive cropping, which favour the disease.

pesticides.application: Paint onto fresh pruning wounds immediately after cutting, per the product label. There is no curative trunk fungicide; trunk injections may only suppress symptoms in some regions and are not a cure.

diseases.description: Grape leaf blight, also known as Isariopsis leaf spot, causes necrotic lesions on grape leaves.
symptoms: Premature leaf drop in severe cases
visual_signs: Irregular brown spots with darker margins
sources: IFV (Institut Français de la Vigne et du Vin)
treatment: Remove and destroy infected leaf litter — the fungus overwinters on fallen leaves.
Maintain an open canopy with positioning and leaf removal to lower humidity around the fruit zone.
Apply protectant sprays during the growing season where the disease is active in warm, humid climates.

pesticides.application: Protectant sprays on green canopy at label intervals during warm, wet periods; rotate copper with mancozeb or a DMI group. Observe the PHI and copper limits under organic rules.

diseases.description: Grape leaf tissue with no visible symptoms of the diseases supported by this model.
Huanglongbing (HLB), or citrus greening, is a devastating bacterial disease transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid. It causes yellowing, misshapen fruit, and eventual tree decline.
visual_signs: Blotchy yellow mottle on one side of the leaf
Unevenly colored fruit with a distinctive green lopsided appearance
prevention: Remove and replace infected trees in high-pressure areas
management: Nutritional support to slow decline (does not cure)
sources: University of Florida IFAS — Citrus Greening
California Department of Food and Agriculture
treatment: There is no known cure: infected trees remain infected and decline. Regional programs typically require roguing — remove and destroy infected trees.
Control the Asian citrus psyllid vector (Diaphorina citri): monitor with yellow sticky traps and shoot inspections.
Manage new flush to reduce psyllid breeding synchrony; remove weeds that host psyllids.
Use only certified clean nursery stock; reflective mulches deter psyllids.
Foliar micronutrient programs (zinc, manganese, iron) can maintain productivity of mildly infected trees but do not remove the bacterium.

pesticides.category: Insecticide (psyllid vector control — does not cure infected trees)
pesticides.application: Target psyllids on new flush: soil-applied neonicotinoids (imidacloprid, clothianidin) at the labelled seasonal soil rate, timed foliar carbaryl or thiamethoxam for adults during flush, plus kaolin or reflective mulch. Vector control protects healthy trees only. Neonicotinoid rules differ widely by country — confirm local registration.

diseases.description: Bacterial spot of peach and nectarine is caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni, producing leaf lesions, fruit spots, and gummosis.
symptoms: Shot-hole appearance as tissue falls out
visual_signs: Angular leaf lesions often limited by veins
treatment: Plant resistant cultivars — the most effective long-term control.
Avoid working among trees when foliage is wet; bacteria spread on tools and clothing.
Apply copper during dormancy to reduce overwintering inoculum, and streptomycin at shuck split where the local label allows it on stone fruit.
Maintain balanced nutrition (avoid excess nitrogen) and provide windbreaks to reduce the leaf tearing that creates infection sites.

pesticides.application: Dormant applications plus cover sprays per label at infection periods; watch for phytotoxicity at high temperatures or concentrations.

Apply at shuck split and per label during warm, wet weather. Antibiotics on fruit crops are restricted in many countries (not permitted in the EU); confirm local registration and resistance-management rules.

diseases.description: Peach leaf tissue with no visible symptoms of the diseases supported by this model.
Bacterial spot of pepper causes leaf, stem, and fruit lesions, reducing plant vigor and fruit quality.
symptoms: Small dark leaf spots with yellow halos
management: Cultural practices to reduce leaf wetness
treatment: Use certified healthy seed and transplants — seed and seedlings are the main entry route.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 1-2 years and remove crop debris after harvest.
Avoid overhead irrigation and working wet foliage; irrigate at the base in the morning.
Apply copper-based bactericides protectively during wet weather, before infection spreads through the canopy.

pesticides.application: Weekly or per-label cover sprays during warm, rainy periods; copper is protectant — it must be on the leaf before infection. Avoid tank-mixes that raise phytotoxicity and respect the PHI.
Mostly greenhouse or transplant programmes where registered; not permitted in the EU. Rotate with copper and follow local resistance-management rules.

Early blight is a fungal disease of potato caused by Alternaria solani, producing dark, target-like lesions on older leaves.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (target pattern)
Lesions begin on older, lower leaves
management: Fungicide programs beginning at canopy closure
treatment: Rotate with non-host crops (not tomato, potato or pepper) for 2-3 years — inoculum builds on debris.
Bury or remove infected vines and volunteer plants.
Maintain a vigorous canopy with balanced nitrogen and regular irrigation; stress and senescence trigger infection.
Hill or mulch to keep developing tubers covered from soil splash.
Apply protectant fungicide once symptoms appear and continue on a label interval until vines senesce.

pesticides.application: Protectant schedule from first symptoms (often at tuber initiation) at 7-14 day intervals per label with full canopy coverage including lower leaves; alternate multi-site products (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) with single-site strobilurins to manage resistance.

diseases.description: Late blight is a destructive oomycete disease caused by Phytophthora infestans that can rapidly destroy potato foliage and tubers.
symptoms: White fungal growth on leaf undersides in humid conditions
treatment: Destroy all inoculum sources: remove and bury or burn cull piles, volunteer potatoes and nightshade weeds — green inoculum near the field is a classic epidemic start.
Plant certified seed and resistant or tolerant varieties suited to local races.
Use ridges and drip irrigation; avoid overhead irrigation and prolonged leaf wetness.
Scout daily in warm, humid weather and use forecast-driven warning systems; at first symptoms remove infected plants and tighten the spray interval.
Delay harvest appropriately after haulm destruction to protect tubers.

pesticides.application: This is an oomycete: multi-site protectants (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) must be on foliage before infection and cannot cure lesions. Rotate in oomycete-specific systemic products (mefenoxam, dimethomorph, cyazofamid, mandipropamid) — mefenoxam resistance is widespread, so never rely on it alone. Spray at 5-7 day intervals under epidemic pressure and observe the PHI.

Powdery mildew on squash and cucurbits is caused by Podosphaera xanthii and produces white powdery growth on leaves.
symptoms: White powdery fungal growth on upper leaf surfaces
visual_signs: White powdery coating that can be rubbed off
management: Fungicide applications (sulfur, horticultural oils, or registered products)
treatment: Choose resistant or tolerant varieties — the most common control.
Space plants for airflow; powdery mildew thrives in dense canopies with warm days and humid nights and, unlike most fungi, does not need free leaf wetness.
Remove badly affected lower leaves as the season progresses and avoid excess nitrogen.
Apply fungicide at the first sign on lower leaves and continue to protect fruit set; spray both leaf surfaces thoroughly.

pesticides.application: Start at first signs at label intervals (typically 7-14 days); rotate the systemic DMIs (myclobutanil, difenoconazole) with contact options (sulfur, potassium bicarbonate, oil, biologicals) to limit resistance. Avoid sulfur plus oil combinations and applications above about 32 C to prevent plant damage; respect the PHI.

diseases.description: Leaf scorch of strawberry is caused by Diplocarpon earlianum, producing irregular purplish-red to brown leaf lesions.
symptoms: Leaf margins turning brown and dry
management: Fungicide applications in autumn and spring
treatment: Remove and destroy infected leaves; renovate heavily affected plantings after harvest (mow, remove old crowns, fertilise to stimulate healthy regrowth).
Renew the planting on a 2-3 year cycle using certified clean transplants.
Mulch to reduce splash and keep foliage dry; irrigate with drip rather than overhead.
Apply fungicide protectively in fall and spring — infection occurs in both periods on young leaves.

pesticides.application: Protectant sprays from post-harvest renovation through fall, and again from late dormancy, at label intervals (often 7-14 days); alternate multi-site captan with DMI or SDHI single-site groups. Mind rain-fastness and the PHI on ripe fruit.

diseases.description: Strawberry leaf tissue with no visible symptoms of the diseases supported by this model.
Bacterial spot of tomato is caused by several Xanthomonas species and produces small, dark lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit.
visual_signs: Dark angular spots limited by veins
treatment: Use certified seed and healthy transplants; treat saved seed with the hot-water or copper protocol from your extension service.
Rotate with non-host crops for 1-2 years and remove all tomato debris after harvest.
Avoid overhead irrigation and splash; mulch at the base and irrigate in the morning so leaves dry.
Apply copper protectively during warm, wet weather — before symptoms spread through the canopy.

pesticides.application: Apply protectively at 7-10 day intervals through warm, wet weather with thorough canopy coverage; copper must be present before infection and cannot cure infected tissue. Watch for phytotoxicity in hot weather; respect the PHI.
Used in greenhouse or transplant programmes where permitted (not in the EU); apply at label intervals and rotate with copper to limit resistance.

diseases.description: Early blight is a common fungal disease of tomato caused by Alternaria solani, producing target-like lesions on older leaves.
symptoms: Dark brown lesions with concentric rings
management: Fungicide applications starting at first symptoms
treatment: Mulch at planting and stake or prune up the plant to block soil splash — most infection comes from debris-borne spores splashed onto lower leaves.
Remove the lowest infected leaves as they appear and destroy debris after harvest.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2-3 years and avoid dense spacing.
Apply protectant fungicide from the first lesions, focusing on the lower canopy, and continue on a label interval through fruit set.

pesticides.application: Start when first lesions appear (or preventively in humid regions) at 7-14 day intervals with excellent lower-canopy coverage; alternate multi-site protectants with single-site products (azoxystrobin, boscalid) to slow resistance and observe the chlorothalonil day-to-harvest restriction.

diseases.description: Late blight of tomato is a fast-spreading oomycete disease that can destroy foliage and fruit within days under cool, wet conditions.
visual_signs: Dark, expanding lesions often starting at leaf tips or margins
treatment: At first symptoms remove and destroy infected plants or leaves immediately — bag them, do not compost.
Eliminate inoculum sources: rogue volunteer tomatoes, potatoes and nightshade weeds; remove cull piles.
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base in the morning and space or prune for rapid drying.
Apply protective fungicide before infection when cool, humid weather is forecast; tighten to a 5-7 day interval during active pressure.
Choose resistant varieties for plantings where the disease recurs.

pesticides.application: Oomycete programme: multi-site protectants (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, copper) applied before rain on a 5-7 day interval under epidemic pressure; rotate in oomycete-specific systemic products (mefenoxam, dimethomorph, cyazofamid) — mefenoxam resistance is common, so do not rely on it alone. Observe the harvest interval.

diseases.description: Tomato leaf mold is a fungal disease common in greenhouses, caused by Passalora fulva (formerly Cladosporium fulvum), producing yellow upper leaf surfaces and olive-green mold on undersides.
symptoms: Pale yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces
Olive-green to brown mold on lower surfaces
visual_signs: Velvety olive-green fungal growth on leaf undersides
management: Fungicide applications (registered products for leaf mold)
treatment: Reduce humidity — the driver of leaf mold: ventilate greenhouses, widen spacing, water at the base and avoid evening leaf wetness.
Resistant varieties (Ve genes) exist for greenhouse production.
Remove and destroy infected lower leaves as symptoms appear.
Scout under the canopy: yellow blotches on the upper leaf surface with olive-brown velvety sporulation underneath signal the start of the epidemic.

pesticides.application: Greenhouse protectant programmes at 7-10 day intervals from first symptoms, with thorough underside coverage because sporulation occurs on the leaf underside; alternate DMI and contact groups; observe the PHI on fruiting crops.

diseases.description: Septoria leaf spot is a fungal disease caused by Septoria lycopersici, producing numerous small circular leaf lesions with dark margins and tan centers.
symptoms: Dark brown margins with tan or gray centers
treatment: Mulch immediately and stake or prune to block splash and speed leaf drying.
At the first small round spots with grey centres, remove the lowest infected leaves and destroy debris after harvest.
Rotate 2-3 years with non-hosts and avoid overhead or evening irrigation.
Apply protectant fungicide once symptoms are present and repeat per label through the season.

pesticides.application: 7-14 day cover sprays from first symptoms with full canopy, especially lower-leaf, coverage; rotate multi-site protectants with single-site products and mind the PHI and re-entry intervals.

diseases.description: Two-spotted spider mites are arachnid pests that feed on tomato leaf cells, causing stippling, bronzing, and webbing.
symptoms: Fine white or yellow stippling on leaves
Fine webbing on leaf undersides and stems
treatment: Conserve predators: lady beetles, minute pirate bugs and especially predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis) control two-spotted spider mite — avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that flare mite populations.
Remove weeds and crop debris that harbour mites and wash dust off foliage — dust favours mites.
Monitor with a beat test: tap foliage over white paper; moving mites plus pale stippling on leaves confirm presence.
Act at threshold (stippling spreading upward); populations explode in hot, dry weather.

active_ingredients: insecticidal soap (potassium salts of fatty acids)
pesticides.application: Spray thorough coverage of leaf undersides every 5-7 days per label while populations build; contact action only, so repeats are needed. Avoid applying in hot sun or soon after sulfur residues (phytotoxicity).

Apply to the leaf underside at labelled intervals, rotating modes of action with the softer options to delay resistance; in greenhouses, releasing predatory mites instead of miticides is preferred where possible. Some products differ by country — confirm local registration.

diseases.description: Target spot of tomato is caused by Corynespora cassiicola and produces brown leaf lesions with concentric rings, similar in appearance to early blight.
symptoms: Lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit
visual_signs: Target-like lesions with alternating light and dark bands
treatment: Remove and bury or destroy crop debris after harvest — the fungus survives on residue.
Rotate with non-host crops for 1-2 years.
Stake and prune for airflow, mulch to reduce splash and avoid working wet foliage.
Apply protectant fungicide from first symptoms during warm, humid weather.

pesticides.application: 7-14 day cover sprays per label from first symptoms with full canopy coverage, rotating multi-site and single-site groups; observe the PHI before harvest.

diseases.description: TYLCV is a geminivirus transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). It causes severe leaf curling, yellowing, and stunting of tomato plants.
symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of young leaves
treatment: No cure exists: remove and destroy infected plants promptly to reduce inoculum in the field.
Control whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci), which spread the virus; monitor with yellow sticky traps.
Use reflective mulches and insect screens in protected cultivation to repel whiteflies.
Plant resistant varieties where available, remove weed hosts around the field and delay planting to avoid peak whitefly pressure.

pesticides.category: Insecticide (whitefly vector control — does not cure infected plants)
pesticides.application: Treat transplants and new growth at label intervals, rotating neonicotinoids, insect growth regulators (pyriproxyfen) and botanicals to avoid resistance; combine with reflective mulch and screens. These protect healthy plants only. Resistance-breaking virus strains exist, so follow local varietal advice.

diseases.description: Tomato mosaic virus is a highly stable plant virus transmitted by mechanical contact, seed, and contaminated tools. It causes mottled leaf patterns and fruit deformation.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green leaf patterns
Irregularly shaped fruit with internal browning
prevention: Disinfect tools and hands between plants
treatment: No cure and no pesticide: remove and destroy infected plants immediately (bag them; do not compost).
Hygiene stops the spread: wash hands with soap and disinfect tools, stakes and hands with trisodium phosphate (10%) or a dilute bleach solution between plants.
Use certified virus-free seed and transplants; mosaic viruses can be seed-borne, so test saved seed.
Do not smoke or handle tobacco just before working in the crop — tobacco can carry the virus onto hands and leaves.
Remove Solanaceae weed hosts around the field and plant resistant varieties where available.
